item.title: Sexual Communication: Unpacking Motivation and Intent
item.description:
Sex

Sexual Communication: Unpacking Motivation and Intent

Why understanding sexual desire goes beyond surface-level wants

Posted July 22, 2026

Key points
  • Sexual behaviors often reflect deeper emotional needs.
  • Motives like validation or insecurity can drive actions.
  • Understanding sexual motivation and intent is key to authentic communication and psychological freedom.

This is Part 2 in a series. Read Part 1 here.

Sexual Representation and Communication Toward Psychological Freedom: Motivation and Intent

How do we arrive at the kind of sex we desire? How do we enable freedom in sexual expression? How do we convey what we want and know to be true about our likes and dislikes? These questions can often be answered by first understanding what we are truly motivated by, which is reflected in our sexual behaviors and communication.

Romantic relationships and sex are significant topics for most people, as reflected in popular media. Humans often use sex to communicate nonsexual issues, and vice versa. For example, excuses like “Honey, I have a headache” or excessive pornography use may signal deeper relationship concerns. Sexual needs and behaviors reveal unique fantasies and desires for each individual.

At times, sex becomes transactional, serving as a means to fulfill unrelated desires, such as exchanging sex for financial security. While sex can meet physical and relational needs, it may also be used to cope with vulnerability, shame, or insecurity. This is common among those who seek connection through multiple partners, often avoiding deeper relational needs and fears.

Sex can facilitate closeness, but the resulting fulfillment is often temporary. A lack of sexual response may reflect our feelings toward a partner or our current life circumstances, with the body expressing what the mind cannot. Difficulties such as inability to orgasm may stem from broader feelings of unfulfillment, fear of aggression, or discomfort with loss of control. Sexual dysfunction can often reveal underlying emotional truths.

Casual sex can become problematic if it leads to reduced pleasure, excitement, or increased feelings of boredom and isolation. These experiences often prompt self-reflection and may lead individuals to seek therapy for loneliness or emptiness, recognizing that sex is no longer providing emotional support. At this point, questions about authentic sexual expression become important. What do you truly want?

What Do We Want?

Freedom in sexual expression requires deep reflection on the purpose sex serves for us. Orgasm is the ultimate release, uniting body and mind in a state of bliss and freedom.

Intent and motivation are complex, especially in sexuality (see Part 1 of this series). Understanding what drives us is essential. Is sex purely about pleasure, or does avoidance indicate deeper guilt or shame? For some, past trauma shapes adult sexual behaviors, such as seeking pleasure through submission or control. Individuals may express dominance or passivity differently in sexual contexts. Some use sex to compensate for inadequacy, while others treat it as a competition or use others solely for gratification.

If we understood our needs and preferences before entering sexual relationships, open communication with partners would likely be more common.

A subtle example can illustrate how sex may serve as a metaphor or vehicle for expressing unrelated emotions, sometimes involving others in this process.

Chelsea and Steve, a married couple, are walking down the street in Anywhere, USA, when an unfamiliar woman approaches them. The woman is determined to make eye contact with Steve, whom she flirts with from several yards away. Steve sends a flirtatious look back. The woman then looks at Chelsea and gives her a soft smile; Chelsea looks at the woman with a complex, shocked expression.

What can we infer from this scenario? As discussed, envy and intent can play significant roles. Even without knowing the motivations, a disruption has occurred. In my experience, individuals often seek to ‘win’ another’s attention, but the true target is frequently the partner observing the interaction.

The scenario with Chelsea and Steve is not about sex itself, but about using sexual behavior to achieve other goals, such as aggression, validation, or resolving relational dynamics. For example, Chelsea may feel marginalized by Steve’s actions. In other cases, the partner observing the interaction may respond with dominance or ridicule, sending a clear message of aggression or self-protection. And sometimes it is a pleasurable fantasy that both partners have agreed to play; however, this can be tricky, as there are often other underlying motivations to this “game.”

Sexual behavior is deeply connected to all aspects of our psychological and relational lives. Understanding what drives our sexual responses requires more than focusing on sex alone. Achieving psychological freedom involves recognizing our motivations or being open to discovering them. Even if our actions do not change, awareness of our underlying motives is essential.

In analysis, we recognize that behavior is multi-determined. There are often multiple, sometimes conflicting, reasons for our actions, feelings, thoughts, and responses in relationships.

Each person experiences multi-determinism differently. I recall a dream shared with me that illustrates how personal meaning can vary greatly.

Sam, a young adult, is struggling with having and maintaining an erection during partnered sex. He dreams that his parents, who are young adults, are lying in bed, and that an elongated, blue-and-red, vein-like object lies between them, with a consistency like firm Jello.

“Holy Freud,” some would say, and would directly and certainly connect the “object” with the man’s penis, vying for the Oedipal position with his mother. Some analysts would unequivocally assume this interpretation: it was Sam’s penis between his mother and father.

Upon further analysis, Sam revealed that the object in the dream represented himself as a developing fetus, symbolizing his desire for nurturing and psychological immaturity. This dream reflected his need for care and development before fully embracing adulthood.

Freud was correct that humans are a complex web of instinctive wishes and the need for fulfillment, but often this need is for love, comfort, and safety amid our vulnerability throughout life.

As adults, we seek to integrate sexual experiences, lovemaking, and psychological intimacy.

Connecting the Sexual Dots

When we recognize, accept, and express our true needs and feelings, we can pursue what we need in sex, relationships, and life.

Achieving honest sexual expression can be a lengthy process. Topics such as politics, religion, illness, family issues, and finances are often easier to discuss now than in the late 20th century, and men are more open about erectile issues. While sexual communication is improving, discussing preferences, fantasies, and compatibility remains challenging for many. People often understand technology more easily than human sexual anatomy. Many heterosexual men are unfamiliar with aspects of female anatomy and arousal, and women may also lack knowledge about their own bodies or fear judgment when discussing these topics. Men may feel ashamed to express their preferences or sensitivities during sex.

Statistics show that anorgasmia affects 16 to 18 percent of women in many countries (psychologytoday.com), and erectile dysfunction impacts about 30 million men in the U.S., or roughly 1 in 10 (clevelandclinic.com). Excluding medical causes, most orgasm difficulties are psychological. Trauma or depression can affect sexual functioning, but even those without such histories often struggle to communicate about sex.

I have worked over the years with couples who have never discussed their sexual preferences or fantasies. Expanding communication to include sex can transform relationships, but openness takes time. Barriers such as poor communication, mistrust, shame, role expectations, and concerns about compatibility are common. Developmental issues, resentment, or conflicts about gender identity can also hinder sexual and psychological freedom.

Sexual needs evolve over time, much like other aspects of our lives. Maintaining awareness of our psychosexual journey requires ongoing self-reflection and communication with partners. Letting go of past sexual identities is part of achieving psychological freedom. While techniques and abilities may change, experience often brings greater fulfillment.

item.title: What Is the Post-Truth Era and Is There Any Truth to It?
item.description:
Media

What Is the Post-Truth Era and Is There Any Truth to It?

Critically thinking about how we engage informational sources.

Posted July 22, 2026

The "post-truth era" refers to a current trend in the zeitgeist, particularly in the media and political landscapes, in which it has been speculated that emotional appeals and personal beliefs have become more influential on public opinion than facts.

I say zeitgeist here because I’m not convinced that such speculation spreads across all of society in a manner that infiltrates "good-thinking" people. People with a basic understanding of epistemology are aware that facts should outweigh emotions and beliefs as sources of evidence, and, as good thinking still exists, I’m confident that this refers to the many, if not most.

However, that doesn’t mean that post-truth hasn’t infiltrated a larger-than-it-should cohort or that we might see "good thinkers" fall prey to such post-truth approaches more often than they should. However, I do think the potential for this speculation to have weight is more widespread than simply relegating it to a pop culture issue. So, I think ‘zeitgeist’ is a good fit—the spirit of this unfortunate possibility is certainly manifest in the background of things.

With that, we’ve seen the use of emotional appeals and the exploitation of personal beliefs for decades, if not centuries, in political argumentation and media representation. Why? It works. I still remember those starving children that Sally Struthers spoke about in the ‘80s and ‘90s. Even the smartest among us are susceptible to fall for such strategies when the conditions are right (at least, in terms of implicit influence). Acknowledgment of such strategies’ power to shape opinion is not new and certainly pre-dates the suggested 2016 start date of the "post-truth era," though I think 2016 is worth mentioning because it also corresponds with the first uses of the phrase fake news.

What does the post-truth era really mean? Is it an explanation for all the poor thinking presented in ‘social’ settings over the past while (be it in vivo public or widely accessible online)? Is it a condemnation of what thinking and sourcing evidence is becoming? Or is it implying that this is just the nature of things now and that we’re as well just accept it? I’m hopeful that it’s a mix of the first two…

And why the focus on media and politics? Whatever you want to say about politics (and regular readers of this blog will know I dislike politics), the focus on media is perhaps most interesting because the issue may be what’s amplifying the effects of other considerations. That is, over the past 10-20 years, we’ve gradually seen the decline of traditional new media. While there are still ‘real’ journalists out there, they represent the minority, given that anyone can be a journalist these days, just as long as they have access to the internet. Buy a website or find a similar platform, start a blog and spew whatever beliefs, opinions and attitudes you have, as if they were factual. Damn bloggers…

Say what you will about traditional news sources, there remained an element of journalistic integrity with reporting, even if there was a slant to the message that came across. But now, when anyone can post whatever they want and dress it up like a credible media source, there’s a lot more room for misinformation, disinformation and generally creating partisanship in societal and political views. Such developments also occur at a time where the internet, particularly social media algorithms, curates personalised experiences for each of its users - echo chambers of perspectives that create collections of siloed information. You see what you like, which may conflate how ‘shared’ such a perspective might be. Likewise, you see things that you hate (i.e. rage bait), thus reinforcing your positive association with the things you do like - strengthening the belief in a bi-partisan reality. There doesn’t seem to be room anymore for centrist political views or reasonable discussion between groups on social media.

While I’d argue that the scope of ‘post-truth’ can apply to fields extending beyond media and politics, it remains that most things can be politicised; and media simply acts a vehicle for information-sharing regarding such topics. For example, if a new scientific finding is released, it may inspire, open up more questions and potential research; or, it may get shot down because it ‘seems’ counter to one’s beliefs that are often linked with a political ideology (e.g. cosmological research, human biology and climate change research), despite affecting everyone regardless of belief or political ideology. Likewise, media can grossly bastardise what scientific findings imply and sensationalise it to sell copies/subscriptions.

The critical thinker would say, if you’re interested in learning about what the new research says, read the original article. But, as I discussed in a previous piece on this blog, who actually does that? We want our information fast, because that’s what the internet/social media has normalised for us—now and quickly. So, we misinterpret the research. We buy into the sensationalisation and we get the wrong message. We grow distrust. When we do hear actual researchers and scientists communicate, they use cautious words like ‘may’, ‘might’, ‘suggest’, ‘perhaps’ and ‘potential’ because good science is rightfully cautious. That doesn’t sound confident. People like confident. They want assuredness. But, that’s not what science is about. Science doesn’t prove anything, rather, it suggests and indicates in light of findings. Be that as it may, further distrust in science and credible institutions grows.

Then we hear something that sounds right, something that we like, that is consistent with what we think already. It piques our confirmation bias. We accept it. We adopt a ‘makes-sense’ epistemology. So, here we are.

So, what do we do? As you’d imagine from a blog about critical thinking, I’m going to recommend that critical thinking is vital to overcoming the many negative implications associated with this ‘post-truth era’ and that we need to make efforts to enhance it in our schools and society. Critical thinking and the ability to evaluate claims and the credibility of information sources go hand in hand. That’s what the public needs to do. But what can those who already think critically do? What can experts, especially in science fields, do? In addition to their research, they need to work to restore the trust of wider society. They need to work to communicate directly with them and work to improve the accessibility of the way they communicate. They need to work to make the ‘post-truth era’ merely a blip in human existence.

item.title: Ruled by Fearthought?
item.description:
Fear

Ruled by Fearthought?

Fears often overrule deliberation and forethought.

Posted July 22, 2026

Key points
  • Competing social selves or identities make some people feel torn all the time.
  • Forethought is the ability to meet competing demands and their effects.
  • Fearthought involves remote, distant, or overblown fears governing a person’s thoughts and actions.
  • Optimism is the antidote to fearthought.

What happens when someone feels torn by their own competing demands? We all have different social selves or identities: we may be parents, children, spouses, co-workers, friends, etc. Each of these selves or identities comes with a host of demands and expectations, not all of which can be met. Even though each demand may be legitimate and capable of being met in principle, they cannot all be met in practice.

Even as we understand the impossibility of meeting them all, some people will continue to try to do so. While others may place demands on us, we place them most heavily on ourselves.

Let’s imagine Ryan, who is a parent of young kids, a dutiful child to their own parents, a good friend, and a hardworking and loyal employee. They’ve always been an optimist, but they’re feeling more and more exhausted; their body aches every day. They can’t really engage in any of their interests anymore. Those interests seem more like luxuries. They feel their spiritual self shrinking a bit; they’re losing interest in a few of their hobbies and can’t justify putting the effort into them.

Their optimism might start to dim, which may feel utterly alien to them. Ryan’s the sort who will just work harder. In the process, they’re more stressed and starting to feel less like themself. Ryan doesn’t recognize the tired and angry face in the mirror. Ryan, like millions of others, may look to alcohol, other drugs, or addictive behaviors to soothe, calm, escape, or provide a temporary reprieve from parts of their self and reality. Ryan may dull the edges of their own knives of fear, disappointment, and resentment.

Forethought versus fearthought

Horace Fletcher (1849-1919), a writer in the American mind-cure movement in the late 1800s, would claim fear is an important catalyst in Ryan’s changing life. While fear serves important roles for each of us individually and for us as a species collectively, it tends to spread. The line between legitimate and illegitimate fears becomes far too porous. Our forethought is our ability to be planful and deliberate about justified fears in particular and the future in general.

People start to suffer when they start anticipating and planning around fears that are remote, imaginary, or over-blown. Our forethought, Fletcher claims, becomes fearthought. When fearthought governs our lives, we are susceptible to high degrees of self-inflicted suffering. Fear affects our bodies in a whole host of ways to the point of wreaking havoc.

In heightened states of fear, more fear takes root. Fear has a way of widening cracks between social selves and hardening our spiritual selves. This tends to breed more fear, creating a cycle that can be difficult to identify and then transform.

What is the flavor of Ryan’s fearthought? They’re afraid of being found out by others that they aren’t what they appear to be. Others might see that they are not the dedicated employee, the good parent, and the attentive child of elderly parents. The fear is that others will see they just can’t keep it all together.

Ryan’s perhaps equally or even more afraid of finding out their own self. Their self-assessment is already colored by their own fears. Fears are tricksters; they take on a variety of shapes. They are powerful motivators often short-circuiting rational thought and deliberation.

This means Ryan may start to take actions that not only are not helpful but are counterproductive. Ryan may physically push themself too far and end up incapacitated. What they formerly saw as positive opportunities are now chances to make more mistakes and disappoint more people. Ryan becomes adept at projecting their fears about possible outcomes and then acting as if they are realities. Even optimism becomes a generator of fear. What if they get their hopes up and things do not work out well?

Ryan may be terrified that if others discover that they aren’t perfect and can’t do it all, not only will they lose respect, but they’ll see their worthlessness. Ryan decides they should start working harder, longer, and better, and doing better so that no one, including themself, could reach the conclusion they are a failure.

Ryan’s spiritual self starts focusing attention on others or what they imagine others are saying about them. They also start to harbor all sorts of resentments towards others, which feels foreign to them. Ryan really can’t seem to get a handle on their own life, and they’re loath to admit this to anyone. They hate feeling this way, but they’re feeling it more frequently and with greater intensity.

Containing fearthought

Fear presses against Ryan’s optimism. How can they restore that optimism that has been the keynote of their life? Fletcher’s diagnosis about fearthought comes with a recommendation common to many of those writing in the mind-cure movement. Relax, let go, stop assuming so much responsibility that isn’t properly yours, and take responsibility for what is yours.

Mind-cure writers tended to recommend people change their starting points in thinking. Instead of fearing something bad is going to happen or that you will be exposed or found out as a fraud or whatever, begin with a positive thought. Cultivate even a tiny bit of optimism.

Fletcher believed that fear and optimism are opposing forces. Where fear reigns, optimism is nearly extinct. Where optimism reigns, fears are kept in appropriate check and fearthought can’t take root. When a person starts to understand how fearthought is governing more of their life, they have the ability and willingness to bridle that fear. They can fend off a full-blown crisis.

item.title: More Courage Changed My Life
item.description:
Personal Perspectives

More Courage Changed My Life

Personal Perspective: Courage gave me the motivation to take the first step.

Posted July 22, 2026

Source: Anastasia Lashkevich / Pexels

Part Two of a Series

My sense of self-esteem and state of consciousness were so low that I walked around with my head down and my shoulders hunched over—a survival posture some people use to be invisible and symbolically protect their heart. Instead of seeing this as a sign of distress, my parents constantly yelled at me to hold my shoulders back. To appease them, I thrust my shoulders back so dramatically it actually affected the way I walked.

I was terrified of school before I even started. The older kids in my neighborhood told me tall tales about spanking machines, knuckle crushers, and other tortures randomly inflicted on kids for no reason.

As I walked to school each day, my protective "don’t notice me" posture had the opposite effect. It attracted bullies to me like hyenas to a wounded gazelle on the Serengeti. Bullies prey on the weak because they too lack self-esteem. The bullying continued for three years. By fourth grade, however, the bullying subsided. I can't say why, perhaps because I’d learned how to avoid the upper-class students, or I was bigger and no longer looked like an easy mark.

The Bullying Picked Up Again in Fifth Grade

This time it was my own classmates who bullied me. It started when two boys attacked me on the playground. One jumped onto my back and pinned my arms down with his knees while the other socked me in my stomach, knocking my breath out. I fell to the ground and couldn't move for several minutes until I was able to breathe again. This got the attention of the whole class. The boy who hit me bragged that he took me out with one punch (he didn’t bother to share that he had an accomplice).

In the following weeks and months, several boys challenged me to fights, thinking they too could beat me and earn some bragging rights. But this time I wasn’t afraid; I was angry, and my pride made me determined; my peers would not get away with it. My anger grew into the courage to stand up to the bullies and fight back. I asked my Dad, who was a boxing champ in high school, for some fighting lessons, which he gladly provided.

He advised me to avoid punching a person on the nose or under the chin; one would cause a nosebleed, the other could knock them out. Both would get me in trouble, my dad said. Instead, he suggested I hit them as hard as I could on the cheek. "Try to do this on your first punch; it will hurt so much, it will likely end the fight right away." His advice worked. Most fights ended after that first punch. Before the school year was over, word got around that I couldn't be beat, and the bullying ended. Sixth grade was peaceful; my state of consciousness had improved. I even made a new best friend with one of the boys who bullied me the year before.

Courage Can Be Acquired Separately in Each Area of Our Lives

In my experience, gaining courage doesn't transfer automatically to all areas of our lives. We have to achieve it in each area separately (school, work, hobbies, relationships, among others), but once we've achieved it in one area, it does become easier in others.

When I look back to fifth grade, I see that I advanced up the scale of states of consciousness from fear to anger and pride, to courage and finally peace. Finding the courage to stand up for myself was liberating; I stopped fearing school for the first time and came to enjoy it.

Today, whenever I sense some hesitation as I move forward in some area of my life, I remind myself to be courageous. In the meantime, I will continue to study the concept of states of consciousness, but I would like to find more peace, and maybe even joy and enlightenment.
